section.title: AI adoption should move with demonstrated capability
section.deck: Casey Muratori frames his concern about generated software as a race between tool reliability and uncritical deployment.

blocks.question: Was your warning that “vibecoding” could make software worse an accurate prediction?
answer: Muratori immediately qualifies the warning: the bad outcome depends on a pattern that may not become dominant. His concern is people describing a desired product, generating it, and sending it into production without competent review. He distinguishes that from a trained engineer using AI while understanding and checking its output.

The resulting risk depends on two moving forces. One is how quickly AI becomes capable of making better decisions autonomously; the other is how widely it is adopted, by whom, and with how much scrutiny. If capabilities stay adequate for the uses people adopt, he would not expect a major deterioration. If adoption outruns the tools and the users’ ability to judge them, he expects trouble.

He explicitly says he does not know where the situation will be a year later. Although he is personally skeptical of AI, he hopes the tools improve because many people are already using them. In his account, freezing their capability at the current level would leave existing adoption in a worse position. These are conditional judgments in the interview, not a forecast supplied by this book.
blocks.speaker: Casey Muratori

blocks.question: Is your criticism of corporate AI mandates that they push adoption ahead of capability?
answer: Muratori says the joke about Shopify was partly a pun, but his substantive concern is organizational fear of being late. He thinks some companies act as if immediate adoption is compulsory before they have established whether the tools solve their actual problems or improve outcomes.

His proposed alternative is familiar technology evaluation: measure what a tool can do, test it against the organization’s problems, compare the workflow with the previous approach, and adopt when it demonstrates a net benefit. Dedicated teams can run aggressive experiments; that does not mean every team should be required to consume large amounts of AI capacity.

He ends by resisting a comforting story about the past. Software quality was already poor before the AI era, he says. AI can make particular things worse without being responsible for the industry’s preexisting failures. The criticism is therefore about how to improve the quality of the work, not about preserving an idealized earlier industry.
blocks.speaker: Casey Muratori

blocks.title: The two questions in Muratori’s argument
rows: Can the tool reliably perform this work?
Is it being used for tasks beyond that capability?
Can it make appropriate decisions without intervention?
Who reviews the output, and how much do they understand?
Has the workflow produced a measured benefit?
Is adoption being required before that benefit is known?
